newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore stunned by Malaysian freeze.
newsitem.headline: Singapore stunned by Malaysian freeze.

text.p: Singapore reacted with stunned dismay on Thursday to Malaysia's decision to freeze ties over a jibe by Singapore elder statesman Lee Luan Yew.

There was no immediate reaction from the government, which appeared to have thought the row was over after Kuala Lumpur accepted Lee's apology for calling the south Malaysian state of Johor "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Indeed, Singapore media quoted Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong as saying during a visit to Laos earlier this week that it was time for Singapore and Malaysia "to move on" from the row.
"There is a Malay saying that water cannot be separated, even with a knife. This is the nature of our relations with Malaysia," Goh was quoted as saying.
"Our interests are very closely intertwined," he said. "We share a common future, because if one country is badly hit, the other will also be affected."
On Thursday, however, the tone in Singapore was remarkably less optimistic.

"It's a very disappointing development. I think this is going to be a long drawn affair. It's not going to blow over in only a couple of days," said one Singapore stockbroker who asked not to be identified.
Another said Singapore should ask for forgiveness rather than calling, as Goh did, for the Lee jibe to be confined to history and for relations to get back to normal.

"The Malaysians are very gracious in forgiveness when asked for it. If we just say, 'let's get on with things', it just proves we don't understand them," said the broker who asked not to be identified.
Malaysia has generally reacted with prickly offence at any suggestion of insult to its Malay majority, especially from ethnic Chinese like those forming the majority in Singapore.
It sees the ethnic Chinese of Singapore as considering themselves superior to the Malays, harder working and more intelligent.

Lee's Johor jibe, made in an affidavit in pursuit of a libel case against a Singapore opposition politician who fled to the Malaysian city saying he feared for his life at home, was seen as a demonstration of exactly that Singapore Chinese attitude.

One Malaysian newspaper, in a report reprinted in Singapore, said the murder rate in Johor Baru, the Johor capital, was only fractionally higher than in Singapore, which has a reputation of being one of the safest cities in Asia.
In Laos, Goh had said Singapore noted that Malaysia, in accepting Lee's apology, had said that it would take time for the wound to heal.
He said Singapore would take steps to improve ties, but would leave it to Kuala Lumpur to set the pace.
Goh also noted that the Malaysian government had approved plans to replace the causeway linking Singapore to Johor Baru, the Johor state capital, with a bridge.
He said Singapore "would certainly look into it" if asked formally.
Goh also said Singapore was keen to upgrade its rail link to Malaysia with high-speed trains once legal and political problems had been sorted out.
He also said there could be more links between Singapore and Johor once the Malaysian state had completed plans for a new city. These were "worthwhile projects for both sides to pursue".

"There are many things we are working on. After some time, when both sides feel comfortable to resume our dialogue over these projects, I believe we should begin to pursue these projects quite earnestly."
